USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the ongoing high-level negotiations in Washington rather than escalate or concede. We should hold our current tariff posture (10% on ~$200B plus the $50B tranche at 25%) as leverage, press hard for verifiable structural concessions on IP protection, forced technology transfers and enforcement, and lock in China's purchase commitments — but avoid any new escalation or concession while the talks are live. Do not link the Huawei/Meng criminal matter to the trade track in a way that collapses the truce; keep it separate and continue negotiating to a framework before the March 2 deadline.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate-to-low and the direction of travel is favorable to us. China is the party under real pressure: official 2018 GDP of 6.6% was the slowest in ~30 years, Q4 slipped to 6.4%, and December exports fell 4.5% and imports 7.6% as the tariff drag bit (country_health/timeline; China macro + Reuters/CNBC Dec trade data). That gives the US leverage, and Trump has explicitly framed it so. The US economy is holding: industrial production roughly flat around 103 and CPI tame; the record $323B bilateral deficit strengthens the domestic case for demanding structural change. Offsetting concerns that temper the reading: US consumer sentiment dropped to 91.2 in January (from ~100 in September), the 10-yr yield has fallen to ~2.7% on growth/market worries, and the Huawei/Meng extradition fight creates a serious overhang that, if mismanaged, could poison the talks and invite sharper Chinese retaliation (DOJ charged Huawei Jan 28 and requested Meng's extradition the same day; China detained two Canadians in Dec). These are risks to manage, not existential threats. On the action axis, escalation now would be counterproductive — it would contradict our professed negotiation, likely trigger 25%-and-beyond retaliation against US farmers and exporters, and spook already-volatile markets (elevated VIX, sharply lower oil suggesting demand fears) — while outright concession would give away leverage we clearly hold. The disciplined play is to negotiate from strength, using the credible March 2 escalation threat and the underlying Chinese economic weakness to extract commitments, without committing new moves yet.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the current high-level negotiation track without new escalation or new concession commitments. We should stay at the table through the remaining weeks of the 90-day window, defend Huawei and demand Meng Wanzhou's release, and signal willingness to make incremental purchase commitments — but resist conceding on structural/sovereignty issues (forced tech-transfer, enforcement) — while keeping the threat that a breakdown would re-trigger the List 3 hike as a bargain to be avoided by both sides, not a card we play.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high, not existential. US Section 301 tariffs now cover ~$250B of our exports (25% on Lists 1-2, 10% on List 3, with a scheduled rise to 25% on the $200B suspended only for the truce), and firm-level targeting is real — ZTE was crippled by a US component ban and US prosecutors on Jan 28 unsealed charges against Huawei/Meng and formally sought her extradition, with analysts warning export controls could threaten Huawei's survival (CNN/Gavekal). This matches the +0.5 anchor: major export sectors hit, yuan stability pressure (forex reserves fell to an 18-month low of ~$3.05T in October), and firm-level targeting of Huawei. At the same time it is not existential: December exports fell 4.4% (biggest drop in two years) and Q4 GDP slowed to 6.4%, but we still posted a record $323B surplus with the US, the yuan rebounded above 6.80 in January on truce optimism, and talks are actively ongoing — evidence we have room to manage rather than a collapse. The action stance follows: because escalation (broad retaliation) would hand Washington the excuse to impose the 25% List 3 hike and deepen the Huawei decoupling — making a bad situation materially worse for our exporters and our technology-independence program — the disciplined move is to hold and negotiate now while keeping purchase-leverage in reserve. We should not yet concede purchases (no matching US rollback is on the table, and the US just escalated on Huawei), so the calibrated stance is neutral negotiate, not rollback.
